title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Aviation
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Three airports lost runway capacity to drones in a week — and one of the drones was carrying explosives
items.content_text: On the night of 5–6 August 2026 an airport worker at Leipzig/Halle found a drone carrying an explosive device near the south runway; the detonator had separated, preventing detonation, and an EOD robot removed it. Both runways closed temporarily and flights diverted. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described it as a new quality of danger and a possible hybrid-attack scenario. On 11 August a drone closed Hannover-Langenhagen’s airspace for over two hours; Der Spiegel reported that police counter-drone detection systems failed to register it, suggesting a non-commercial airframe. On 11–12 August a departing Boeing 777 spotted a drone at 1,800 ft near Ho Chi Minh City’s Tan Son Nhat, and a second sighting closed Vietnam’s busiest airport for over two hours, grounding or diverting at least 22 flights. These are physical and hybrid incidents rather than cyber compromises of airport systems — but they hit the same target that a cyber attack on airfield systems would, and the Hannover detection failure is a control gap, not a policy one.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Leipzig/Halle and Hannover authorities, Vietnamese aviation authorities — via NPR, Der Spiegel

items.title: NTSB is investigating a fatal medevac crash that followed GPS loss during a military jamming exercise
items.content_text: The NTSB is investigating the crash of a Beechcraft King Air C90 medevac aircraft into New Mexico’s Capitan Mountains on 14 May 2026, which killed two pilots and two nurses. The aircraft lost GPS signal during an active military GPS-jamming exercise at White Sands; three other aircraft reported GPS loss the same night. Be precise about what is established: the NTSB confirms the jamming exercise took place and that GPS was lost, but has not determined probable cause or contributing factors, so any causal link remains unproven. The context is a documented global rise in GNSS interference — the FAA’s updated GPS/GNSS Interference Resource Guide (v1.1, April 2026) cites a 65% year-on-year increase in GPS signal loss per 1,000 flights and eight persistent jamming and spoofing hotspots worldwide.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: NTSB investigation — via Stars and Stripes; FAA GPS/GNSS Interference Resource Guide v1.1

items.title: Attackers took hands-on control of water-utility PLCs across a dozen states — locking out operators and knocking a treatment plant offline
items.content_text: Between 26–27 July 2026 a coordinated campaign disrupted automated controls at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems, and confirmed intrusions have since been reported across roughly a dozen states including Georgia, Michigan, South Dakota, Alabama and New Jersey. This is hands-on manipulation of control equipment, not a data breach: CISA says the actors changed PLC passwords and altered device IP addresses to lock operators out of their own equipment. In Braham, Minnesota a pump failure forced a treatment facility offline and prompted a resident conservation notice; Clayton County, Georgia issued a precautionary boil-water advisory after a pump-station disruption, later lifted. Dragos’s Rob Lee told NPR he could not recall “this many targets at once with operational impact.” Every affected utility reported that drinking water stayed safe, with staff falling back to manual operation. Federal officials have pointed to Iran-linked activity — a TLP:AMBER WaterISAC assessment reportedly found the evidence aligned with campaigns previously attributed to Iran — but no formal public attribution has been made, so treat the actor as suspected rather than confirmed.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA / FBI / EPA, MNIT and affected city statements — via NPR, The Record, Dark Reading, BleepingComputer
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Incidents from 26 Jul 2026; scope reporting through 12 Aug 2026

items.title: Cisco ASA and Firepower join KEV under active exploitation — the OT perimeter is the target again
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-20349, a heap-inspection vulnerability in Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and Firepower Threat Defense software, to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 11 August 2026, citing evidence of active exploitation. The same batch added CVE-2026-68820, a use-after-free in the Windows afd.sys driver enabling local privilege escalation — relevant because Windows engineering workstations and HMI servers are exactly where that gets chained after initial access — and CVE-2026-72898, a SQL injection in Metabase exposing stored credentials. Earlier in the month CISA added CVE-2026-8037, an unauthenticated command injection in Progress Kemp LoadMaster carrying CVSS 9.6, after sustained exploitation attempts, with a federal patch deadline of 10 August under BOD 26-04. None of these are ICS products. All of them sit in front of, or inside, the path into OT.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV catalogue — via The Hacker News, CyberExperts

items.title: An N-able N-central auth bypass was exploited, patched incompletely, then exploited again
items.content_text: CISA added two N-able N-central authentication-bypass flaws to KEV within two days: CVE-2026-18556 and CVE-2026-18577, both CVSS 8.2, the second being an incomplete-fix follow-on to the first. N-able confirmed a limited number of customer breaches. Attackers who exploit it take over administrator accounts and can pivot to managed endpoints through the platform’s Take Control remote-session feature. Huntress reported that 55.6% of reachable cloud servers were still unpatched at the time of its analysis. The fix is 2026.3.1.7 / 2026.3 HF1. RMM platforms matter disproportionately in OT because they are how integrators, machine builders and managed-service providers reach plant equipment — often through a path that was never security-reviewed and does not appear on the network diagram.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA KEV; N-able advisory — via The Hacker News, Help Net Security

items.title: August ICS Patch Tuesday: a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw in Siemens Simatic IoT2050, plus Schneider and Phoenix Contact fixes
items.content_text: Siemens published ten advisories in the August cycle. The headline item is a maximum-severity missing-authentication vulnerability in Simatic IoT2050 Advanced edge devices that a remote, unauthenticated attacker could use to execute code with elevated privileges. Also in the batch: an OS command injection in Siemens Siveillance Video / Milestone XProtect management servers (CVE-2026-3014, CVSS v3.1 9.1, v4.0 6.4) exploitable by users holding edit permissions, and two Siemens License Server flaws — CVE-2026-69108 (CVSS 6.0, local privilege escalation via an insecure sudoers policy) and CVE-2026-69109 (CVSS 7.5, path traversal), fixed in v5.1+ and v5.3+ respectively. Schneider Electric addressed two code/command execution issues in NetBotz 5 and an authentication-attempt flaw in PowerChute Serial Shutdown. Phoenix Contact published a PLCnext firmware advisory covering unauthenticated denial-of-service and malicious SQL query execution.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Siemens ProductCERT, Schneider Electric, Phoenix Contact — via SecurityWeek and CISA ICSA-26-225-07 / -09

items.title: Johnson Controls patched hardcoded credentials in the TL280 communicator and cross-site scripting in Metasys UI
items.content_text: Two Johnson Controls advisories landed in the August cycle. ICSA-26-218-02 covers CVE-2026-27871, hardcoded credentials in the TL280 internet security alarm communicator on firmware below 5.63, which could expose sensitive device data; CISA scores it CVSS v3.1 4.1 / v4.0 2.1 and notes high attack complexity. ICSA-26-225-14 covers a cross-site scripting weakness in the Metasys UI building-automation front end. CISA also issued Update A to its earlier advisory for C-CURE 9000 and victor application servers. Neither individual flaw is dramatic. The reason they belong on an OT page is placement: building automation, access control and alarm communications routinely share network segments with industrial systems while sitting outside the OT patching programme and often outside the OT asset register entirely.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICSA-26-218-02, ICSA-26-225-14, ICSA-26-204-01 Update A

items.title: Aviation’s expensive cyber losses happen on the ground, not in the air
items.content_text: Cyviation chief executive Eliran Almog argues that material aviation cyber losses come from ground systems — reservations, ground handling, MRO IT, crew scheduling — rather than in-flight compromise, while aircraft remain exposed as data endpoints consuming navigation databases and loadable software with limited integrity checking. He flags GNSS jamming and spoofing as effectively invisible to standard SIEM and SOC tooling, which are built around IT telemetry and have no view of the RF environment. His recommendation for smaller carriers is to prioritise multi-factor authentication on ground operations and basic aircraft-visibility tooling over building an in-house security team. It is a vendor perspective and should be read as one, but the ground-systems point matches where every publicly documented aviation disruption of the last two years has actually landed.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Eliran Almog, Cyviation — via Help Net Security

items.title: Ransomware crews and espionage actors both treat aviation as a priority sector
items.content_text: Threat-landscape reporting from CybersecurityNews and PolySwarm describes aviation and aerospace as among the most actively targeted sectors through 2025 and 2026, naming Qilin, LockBit and Cl0p on the extortion side, Scattered Spider for identity-based intrusion and help-desk social engineering, and espionage-focused groups including Refined Kitten, Wicked Panda and Fancy Bear against aerospace and defence-adjacent targets. The incidents most often cited — the Collins Aerospace MUSE passenger-processing compromise in September 2025 and the Qilin attack on Tulsa International Airport in January 2026 — predate this reporting window and are referenced as actor context, not fresh events. The Scattered Spider element deserves attention because the initial access is a phone call to a service desk, and no amount of OT segmentation addresses that.

items.title: Peer-reviewed analysis puts airports’ central vulnerability in their third-party digital dependencies
items.content_text: A study in the Journal of Transportation Security analysing 2024 and 2025 incidents concludes that airports’ heavy dependence on third-party digital services — check-in, baggage handling, public Wi-Fi and airline portals — is the sector’s central vulnerability, citing ransomware against passenger-processing systems and drone intrusions at Copenhagen and Oslo as illustrative cases. The recommendation is coordinated international threat management and shared resilience initiatives. It is included as background rather than news. The value for an operator is the framing: an airport is an integrator of other organisations’ systems on a shared physical site, and its security posture is largely determined by contracts and interfaces rather than by anything inside its own firewall.

items.title: Dragos counted 1,140 industrial ransomware incidents in Q2 — and not one reached stage 2 of the ICS kill chain
items.content_text: Dragos’s Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis recorded 1,140 incidents against industrial organisations, up 12% on Q1. Manufacturing absorbed 747 of them (65%), led by construction at 176 and equipment manufacturing at 114; food and beverage accounted for 70. The finding worth carrying into your own risk conversations is the negative one: Dragos found no case in Q2 where a ransomware operator reached stage 2 of the ICS Cyber Kill Chain. Production stopped because enterprise IT and ERP systems stopped — order entry, scheduling, shipping, labelling — not because anyone touched a controller. Named Q2 cases include West Pharmaceutical Services and Foxconn, the latter with a roughly two-week outage at Wisconsin and Texas sites. That pattern should shape where you spend: the loss is real, but the control is IT/OT dependency mapping and recovery, not deeper controller hardening.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Dragos Q2 2026 Industrial Ransomware Analysis — via Help Net Security

items.title: GAO found TSA has not defined who owns aviation cybersecurity — and is still working from a 2018 roadmap
items.content_text: GAO report 26-107693 examined how the FAA and TSA manage aviation cybersecurity. The FAA has defined cybersecurity roles across seven entities but under-reported cybersecurity costs to OMB for fiscal years 2024 to 2026, and has fully implemented three of seven Zero Trust strategic objectives. The finding against TSA is more serious: GAO says TSA has not clearly defined cybersecurity roles and responsibilities and is still operating from a 2018 Cybersecurity Roadmap that is misaligned with current DHS strategy. GAO issued five recommendations, four to the FAA and one to TSA. For airport and airline operators the practical read is that the agency setting your cyber requirements is itself working from an outdated internal framework — expect requirements to change, and build programmes that can absorb that rather than compliance artefacts tuned to today’s directive text.

items.title: EASA Part-IS now binds air operators, ANSPs and maintenance organisations — full compliance is due August 2027
items.content_text: EASA’s Part-IS regime — Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1645 and Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/203 — requires an information security management system covering risk assessment, incident detection and response, mandatory incident reporting and supply-chain risk evaluation. Air operators, air navigation service providers, maintenance and training organisations and competent authorities came into scope on 22 February 2026, following aerodrome operators and design and production organisations on 16 October 2025. Full compliance across the sector is required by 22 August 2027. The supply-chain evaluation requirement is the one most organisations underestimate: it reaches the ground handlers, MRO providers and IT suppliers whose compromise has caused most real aviation disruption, and it demands documented assessment rather than a signed questionnaire.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: EASA Part-IS — Regulations (EU) 2022/1645 and 2023/203; analysis via Jones Day
_otthreatfeed.date_note: In force from 22 Feb 2026; full compliance 22 Aug 2027

items.title: The FAA finalised a rule requiring interference-tolerant radio altimeters
items.content_text: The FAA published a final rule on 31 July 2026 requiring all US aircraft to be fitted with radio altimeters meeting a new interference tolerance mask standard, so they withstand adjacent-band C-band wireless signals. The stated concern is that RF interference could produce erroneous altitude data feeding navigation and safety systems. Compliance deadlines are 30 December 2030 for major and foreign air carriers and 31 October 2034 for other operators. It is a safety and spectrum rule rather than a cyber advisory, and it is included here for a specific reason: it is a rare case of a regulator mandating hardware-level resilience to RF interference in a safety-critical sensor path, which is the same class of problem as the GNSS interference and unauthenticated RF signalling issues showing up across aviation, rail and maritime.
